theme: Contend for the faith once delivered
readingInstruction: Read Jude, a single chapter. Jude writes with urgency about false teachers who have crept into the church, and ends with one of the most beautiful doxologies in the Bible. Notice the examples from history and the practical instructions in verses 20 to 23.
settingTheScene: Jude, the brother of James and therefore a brother of Jesus (though he calls himself a servant), intended to write about “our common salvation” but found it necessary instead to write a call to defend the faith. People had slipped into the churches who denied Christ’s lordship and turned grace into an excuse for immorality. Jude’s letter is closely parallel to 2 Peter 2. It uses examples from the Old Testament and from Jewish writings of the period.
observation: “Contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (v. 3).
“Pervert the grace of our God into sensuality” (v. 4).
“He did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment” (v. 9).
“Building yourselves up in your most holy faith; praying in the Holy Spirit” (v. 20).
“Keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life” (v. 21).
“And have mercy on those who doubt” (v. 22).
“Save others by snatching them out of the fire” (v. 23).
“Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (v. 24).
interpretation:
Jude introduces himself and greets his readers as “those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ.” Called, loved, kept: three words that summarize the Christian’s security. Then the appeal: “Contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.” The faith is a body of truth, entrusted to the apostles, complete and unchanging. We do not invent it or improve on it, but we guard and defend it. “Contend” is a strong word, like an athlete struggling for a prize, though Paul says the servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome (2 Timothy 2:24). The way to contend is with truth, courage, and compassion.

The danger: “certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.” Their error is two-fold: moral (grace as license) and doctrinal (denying Christ’s lordship). Jude gives three examples of judgment: Israel, who was saved out of Egypt but destroyed when they did not believe; the angels who left their proper place; and Sodom and Gomorrah. Great privilege does not protect those who persist in unbelief.

The false teachers “reject authority and blaspheme the glorious ones.” Jude contrasts them with the archangel Michael, who, even in a dispute with the devil, “did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, The Lord rebuke you.” Jude refers to a tradition about Michael and Moses’ body, probably from a Jewish writing of the time, and to a prophecy of Enoch, which seems to come from the Book of 1 Enoch. Does that make these books Scripture? No. Paul also quoted pagan poets (Acts 17:28) without making them canonical. An inspired author may cite a true statement from a non-inspired source. This is why the canon (see Day 851) is important.

Jude’s descriptions of the false teachers are some of the most vivid in the Bible: “hidden reefs” at the love feasts, “waterless clouds, swept along by winds,” “fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead, uprooted,” “wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame,” “wandering stars for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.” Their end is judgment, as Enoch prophesied. They are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires, loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism for gain.

Then Jude turns to the readers: “But you, beloved, remember the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Scoffers will come. Our response is a fourfold program: “building yourselves up in your most holy faith; praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.” Notice the Trinity: Spirit, God, Lord Jesus. Faith, prayer, love, and hope together keep us in God’s love. And then ministry to others: “And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.” Three types of people receive three types of care: gentleness for the doubting, urgency for the endangered, and cautious compassion for those entangled in sin.

The letter ends with a doxology that has been read at countless services: “Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.” We contend for the faith, but ultimately it is God who keeps us. And he will present us blameless, with great joy.
connection: 2 Peter 2 is a close parallel. Numbers 14 and 26:64-65 record the wilderness generation. Genesis 6:1-4 and 19:1-29 relate to the angels and Sodom. Zechariah 3:2 contains the words “The Lord rebuke you.” Genesis 5:18-24 mentions Enoch. Numbers 16 and 22-24 tell of Korah and Balaam. Genesis 4:3-8 tells of Cain. 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 1:13-14 call us to guard the deposit. Acts 20:28-31 warns of wolves. Romans 16:25-27 is another great doxology. Philippians 1:6 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23-24 offer similar assurance.
application:
Memorize verse 24, and say it at the end of the day as a prayer of trust.

Choose one of the four disciplines in verses 20 and 21 (faith, prayer, love, hope) and strengthen it this week.

Think of a person who doubts. Reach out to them with patience and mercy.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you are called, loved, and kept.
Ask him to help you contend for the faith with truth and love.
Ask him to keep you in his love and show mercy to the doubting.
